title: Foundations and how to read a call
summary: What SIP is for, which network facts it assumes, and how to read a ladder without inventing rules.

lessons.title: What SIP is for
lessons.summary: SIP creates, changes, and ends sessions, while RTP carries the media those sessions describe.
objectives: Separate SIP signaling from RTP media
Name user agent, proxy, registrar, and redirect server
Treat 100 Trying as hop-by-hop quench, not as an answer

illustration.title: Two planes
illustration.caption: SIP agrees the session. SDP names the media. RTP moves the samples.

layers.name: SDP
layers.detail: Offer and answer: address, port, codec

paragraphs: SIP is an application-layer protocol for creating, modifying, and terminating sessions among one or more participants. A phone call is the usual session, and the protocol still does not define the audio coding or the packet format of the voice.

RTP carries the media packets. SDP, carried inside SIP, is the offer and the answer that name the addresses, ports, and codecs. Read RFC 3261 for the signaling rules and keep the media RFCs beside it.

A user agent originates or answers a request. A proxy routes requests and responses. A registrar accepts REGISTER and stores the Contact bindings for an address-of-record. A redirect server answers with a 3xx and leaves the path.

An SBC is usually a back-to-back user agent: it terminates one dialog and creates another. RFC 7092 is the taxonomy, and RFC 5853 collects the deployment requirements. Naming the role in a trace is the useful step. The product logo is not a protocol role.

quiz.q: What does a SIP INVITE carry?
choices: Session signaling, and often an SDP offer
quiz.why: Voice samples are RTP. SDP inside the INVITE names where those samples will go.

quiz.q: Which document is the base SIP specification?
quiz.why: RFC 3550 is RTP, RFC 8866 is SDP, and G.711 is a codec recommendation.

quiz.q: A pure proxy is responsible for
quiz.why: Media handling is B2BUA or media-server behavior. A proxy routes SIP.

quiz.q: A registrar stores
quiz.why: REGISTER creates bindings. Section 10 defines that role.

quiz.q: 100 Trying means
choices: This hop has the INVITE and is quenching retransmissions
quiz.why: A stateful proxy does not forward 100 Trying. It generates its own when it needs to.

quiz.q: An SBC most often behaves as
quiz.why: RFC 7092 classifies SIP B2BUAs. Two dialogs, two Call-IDs, is the usual SBC trace.

cards.back: Application signaling for sessions. The base specification is RFC 3261.
Describes media. Offer/answer is RFC 3264.
Carries the media packets after the answer names the port.
Hop-by-hop provisional. A stateful proxy generates it and does not relay one.

lab.title: Find the offer
lab.prompt: Play the ladder and open the first INVITE. The audio offer is the SDP body, not a later response.
steps: Play the ladder through the first INVITE.
Inspect that INVITE and find the m= line.
Confirm the 100 Trying has no SDP body.

check.q: Where is the first SDP offer on this ladder?
check.why: This ladder is early offer. The INVITE body is the offer.

fault.title: Silence after a clean 200 OK
fault.symptom: The ladder shows 200 OK with SDP, and the caller hears silence.
fault.log:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Type: application/sdp
m=audio 19642 RTP/AVP 0
c=IN IP4 203.0.113.20
(no UDP packets observed on port 19642)
choices: Signaling succeeded and RTP never arrived
The 200 OK is illegal without audio samples
Call-ID must contain the RTP port
ACK is required to carry PCMU frames
fault.why: SDP names the RTP address and port. The samples are a separate flow.
fault.cause: The dialog was established. Nothing was captured on the negotiated media port.
fault.fix: Capture UDP on the c= address and m= port from the answer. Leave the 200 OK alone once those values are known.

lessons.title: Ports, transports, and where a request can go
lessons.summary: SIP uses UDP or TCP on 5060 and TLS on 5061, and a request that does not fit one datagram needs a connection.
objectives: State the default ports for UDP, TCP, and TLS
Explain why a large INVITE moves off UDP
Recognize WebSocket as a transport, not a new method set

illustration.title: Defaults operators meet
illustration.caption: A peer document can override a default. The default is the rule when the peer is silent.
rows: Same methods, WS or WSS in Via

paragraphs: RFC 3261 section 18 sets UDP and TCP on port 5060 and TLS on port 5061. UDP is why INVITE retransmissions exist: the transaction layer repeats a request that may have been lost.

A request that does not fit in one datagram belongs on a connection-oriented transport. TCP and TLS use Content-Length to find the end of the message. WebSocket, RFC 7118, carries the same SIP messages with transport tokens WS and WSS.
A sips URI asks for TLS on the signaling hop. The method names, the dialog rules, and the SDP offer do not change because the Via says TLS.
When a deployment encrypts the media, that keying is negotiated in SDP, for example with DTLS-SRTP. Read the Via transport, the sent-by host, and the port before you argue about certificates.

quiz.q: The default SIP UDP port is
quiz.why: 5061 is the TLS default. Both come from section 18.

quiz.q: The default SIP TLS port is
quiz.why: TLS is still SIP. The port default is 5061.

quiz.q: A SIP request larger than one UDP datagram should
quiz.why: Loss of a fragment looks like a timeout, and the transaction retransmits the same datagram.

quiz.q: RFC 7118 adds
quiz.why: WS and WSS appear in Via. The methods stay the ones you already know.

quiz.q: A sips URI requires
quiz.why: Media protection is negotiated in SDP, not by the URI scheme alone.

quiz.q: On TCP, message framing uses
quiz.why: A stream has no datagram boundary. Content-Length tells the parser where the body ends.

cards.back: Default port for SIP over UDP and SIP over TCP.
Default port for SIP over TLS.
On a stream transport, this is how the parser finds the end of the message.
WebSocket transport tokens from RFC 7118. The SIP methods do not change.

fault.title: INVITE retransmits, TCP works
fault.symptom: A large INVITE on UDP is retransmitted and then times out. The same peer answers when the request is sent on TCP.
fault.log:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.20:5060;branch=z9hG4bKbig1
Max-Forwards: 70
Content-Type: application/sdp
Content-Length: 2100
(three UDP retransmits, no response)
choices: The UDP request is too large for the path
fault.why: Section 18 is why a large request moves to TCP or TLS.
fault.cause: The datagram is not getting a response. The peer answers the same SIP on a stream transport.
fault.fix: Send this peer SIP over TCP or TLS, or shrink the SDP. Keep the method and the dialog rules the same.

lessons.title: E.164, sip URIs, and tel URIs
lessons.summary: A global number is written in a tel URI or in a sip URI user part, and E.164 is the numbering plan those digits follow.
objectives: Read a global tel URI and a sip URI with user=phone
Say what E.164 is without inventing an ITU clause
Keep the Request-URI and the To URI as different fields

illustration.title: Three ways the same number appears
illustration.caption: The digits are the numbering plan. The scheme decides who can route the identifier.
rows: A number plus a SIP domain

sections.h: The number and the URI are different layers
paragraphs: RFC 3966 defines the tel URI. A global number begins with +. The user part of sip:+15551212@example.com is that same kind of number when the URI carries user=phone.

E.164 is the ITU-T numbering plan those digits follow. This course cites RFC 3966 for the URI syntax and does not invent an ITU clause number. When a ticket says E.164, check the digits and the leading +, then check which URI scheme is on the wire.

sections.h: A tel URI has no domain to look up
paragraphs: A tel URI does not name a host, so a SIP element that must forward it builds a sip URI. The telephone-subscriber goes in the user part, and the host becomes the domain that should route it.

The Request-URI is where this hop sends the request. The To header is the logical destination the caller identified. They often look alike on the first INVITE and they diverge as soon as a proxy retargets.

quiz.q: Which document defines the tel URI?
quiz.why: 3966 is the URI. DNS location of a SIP server is 3263.

quiz.q: E.164 is
choices: The ITU-T numbering plan the digits follow
quiz.why: Cite 3966 for the URI. Do not invent an ITU section number for the plan.

quiz.q: user=phone on a sip URI means
choices: Treat the user part as a phone number
quiz.why: The parameter is a hint about the user part. It is not a transport.

quiz.q: A tel URI differs from a sip URI because
choices: It has no host for DNS or a Request-URI target
It cannot contain a plus sign
It creates a dialog by itself
quiz.why: Something in the SIP network has to place that number into a sip URI before RFC 3263 applies.

quiz.q: On the first INVITE, To and the Request-URI
choices: Often match, and a proxy may retarget only the Request-URI
quiz.why: To identifies the logical target. The Request-URI is the routing target for this hop.

quiz.q: The ACK for the 302 uses
choices: The same branch as the INVITE
A new branch, because every ACK is end to end
A To header with the tag removed
quiz.why: 302 is a non-2xx final response. That ACK stays inside the INVITE transaction.

The sip user part should be read as a phone number.
The ITU-T numbering plan. The URI citation in this course is RFC 3966.
Where this hop sends the request. Retargeting changes it and leaves To in place.

fault.title: A tel URI stuck in the Request-URI
fault.symptom: A proxy answers 416 Unsupported URI Scheme to a request whose Request-URI is a tel URI.
fault.log:
INVITE tel:+15551212 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKtel1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl

Call-ID: tel-1@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

SIP/2.0 416 Unsupported URI Scheme
choices: The proxy has no sip URI to route and does not implement tel
The branch cookie is missing a tag
fault.why: A tel URI has no host. An element that cannot use it returns 416 or maps it to a sip URI.
fault.cause: The Request-URI scheme is tel, and this hop has no mapping to a SIP domain.
fault.fix: Map tel:+15551212 to sip:+15551212@example.com;user=phone at the edge that owns the numbering plan, then let RFC 3263 run on example.com.

lessons.title: How to read an RFC
lessons.summary: A SIP argument cites the RFC number and the section, and the normative sentences outrank a broken example.
objectives: Separate Standards Track text from an Informational map
Cite a rule by RFC and section
Use the ABNF and the prose together

illustration.title: Where to open RFC 3261
illustration.caption: Memorize the chapter map. You will use it every time a trace disagrees with a product screen.
rows: A tag or a branch is in question

paragraphs: The top of an RFC tells you the status. RFC 3261 is Standards Track. An Informational RFC can index the others and it does not replace a Standards Track rule.

MUST, SHOULD, and MAY are the requirement words. A SHOULD is a rule you depart from only with a reason you can write down. When an example and a normative sentence disagree, follow the sentence and the ABNF in section 25.
Section 20 is the header catalog. Section 21 is the response codes. Section 7 is how a message is formed, including compact names. Quoting a vendor slide is not a citation.
Do not paste the RFC into a runbook. Paraphrase the rule and link to the RFC editor. The legal terms for the text itself are covered in the licensing lesson.

lessons.summary: RFC 5411 is an informational map of the SIP document set, and it does not replace the base specification.
objectives: Use RFC 5411 as an index

illustration.title: Map, then document
illustration.caption: Start at the map when you do not know which RFC owns a header. Finish in the RFC that defines it.

layers.name: Extension RFC
layers.detail: PRACK, UPDATE, timers, REFER, and the rest

sections.h: An index is not the protocol
paragraphs: RFC 5411 is Informational. It lists the SIP specifications so you can find the document that owned a behavior when the guide was published. It is not a substitute for RFC 3261.

When a header is absent from section 20 of RFC 3261, look for an extension. PRACK is RFC 3262. UPDATE is RFC 3311. Session timers are RFC 4028. REFER is RFC 3515. The guide helps you discover that split.

sections.h: The map stopped. The protocol did not
paragraphs: A snapshot cannot include documents published after it. RFC 6026 corrects INVITE 2xx handling. RFC 6141 tightens target refresh. RFC 6665 is the events specification. RFC 7118 adds WebSocket.

Use 5411 to choose a starting document, then read that document and anything that updates it. If a header is only in the guide's table and not in the extension you implemented, you do not have the rule yet.

fault.cause: The design stopped at the index.
fault.fix: Read the INVITE transaction in RFC 3261 section 17 and the 2xx correction in RFC 6026. Keep 5411 as the list of documents.

lessons.title: Licenses, codecs, and what you may copy
lessons.summary: Protocol text is under the IETF trust provisions, and codec rights have to be read from the codec's own documents.
objectives: Point at the IETF Trust Legal Provisions for protocol text
Separate Opus documents from G.711 and G.729
Refuse to state a patent expiry date

illustration.title: What to open before you ship
illustration.caption: This lesson is not legal advice. It tells you which documents to read.
rows: Paste an RFC into a manual
RFC 6716, the Opus license, IETF IPR
Assume the RFC is the license
Treat it as an IETF RFC
ITU-T G.729 and current patent status
State an expiry date from memory

sections.h: The protocol text has a license
paragraphs: SIP is specified by the IETF. The terms for using that text are the IETF Trust Legal Provisions. Read them before you copy specification text into a product, a course pack, or a customer document.

This course paraphrases rules and links the RFCs. It is not legal advice, and it does not tell you that a particular copy is permitted. If you need a permission, read the trust provisions or ask counsel.

sections.h: Codecs are not the SIP license
paragraphs: Opus is specified in RFC 6716. The license the codec project publishes is at the Opus license page, and patent disclosures are listed in the IETF IPR disclosure system. Read those three. This lesson does not clear a product.
G.711 and G.729 are ITU-T recommendations. Cite those recommendations for the codec. Patent status for G.729 has to be verified against current sources. This course states no expiry date.

lessons.title: Reading the first INVITE
lessons.summary: The first INVITE has a magic-cookie branch, Max-Forwards 70, a From tag, and no To tag.
objectives: Read a request line and the required headers in order
Check the branch cookie and the initial Max-Forwards
Recognize documentation addresses from RFC 5737

illustration.title: First-request checklist
illustration.caption: Miss one row and the transaction or the dialog will not match later.
rows: Local half of the dialog id
The tag arrives on a response

sections.h: The start line and the routing budget
paragraphs: A request starts with the method, the Request-URI, and SIP/2.0. The first Via names the transport and the address where this hop wants the response, and the branch parameter identifies the transaction.

A branch written by an implementation of this specification begins with the magic cookie z9hG4bK. The UAC inserts Max-Forwards, and the initial value SHOULD be 70. Each proxy that forwards the request decrements it by one.

The From header on a request the UAC creates carries a tag. The To header on a request outside a dialog has no tag. Call-ID is the third piece of dialog identity, together with those two tags once the To tag exists.

CSeq is a number plus the method token. Contact on an INVITE is the remote target the answerer will use later. The addresses 203.0.113.10, 203.0.113.20, 198.51.100.30, and 192.0.2.40 are documentation ranges from RFC 5737, not production hosts.

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: Start line, then Via. The branch begins with z9hG4bK. Max-Forwards on a request the UAC creates SHOULD be 70.

Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bK7766as01
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Supported: 100rel,replaces,timer
Allow: INVITE,ACK,CANCEL,BYE,UPDATE,PRACK,OPTIONS,REFER
Content-Length: 218

Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bK7766ack

quiz.q: The branch magic cookie is
quiz.why: Seven characters, defined for the branch in section 8.1.1.7.

quiz.q: The initial Max-Forwards value SHOULD be
quiz.why: The UAC inserts it. Proxies decrement when they forward.

quiz.q: The To header on the initial INVITE
quiz.why: The tag that completes the dialog arrives on a response.

quiz.q: Dialog identity uses
choices: Call-ID, From tag, and To tag
quiz.why: The branch identifies the transaction. The tags identify the dialog.
TEST-NET ranges are for examples. Do not route production traffic at them.

quiz.q: CSeq on this INVITE contains
choices: A number and the method INVITE
quiz.why: Later, ACK uses the same number and the method token ACK.

cards.back: Magic cookie at the start of a branch parameter.
The value a UAC SHOULD put on a request it originates.
An initial request is outside a dialog, so To has no tag.
Documentation IPv4 ranges used for the examples in this course.

check.why: z9hG4bK7766as01 is one transaction id. The cookie is the first seven characters.

fault.title: Branch without the cookie
fault.symptom: A proxy never matches the response to the request. The Via branch is a random token with no cookie.
fault.log:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=7766as01
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Content-Length: 0
choices: The branch does not start with z9hG4bK, so it is not a 3261 transaction id
fault.why: The cookie tells the peer that the branch was built as a unique transaction id.
fault.fix: Generate the branch so it begins with z9hG4bK and is unique for this request. CANCEL and a non-2xx ACK are the cases that reuse the INVITE's branch.
